newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia steps up pressure on Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: Australia steps up pressure on Cambodia.

text.p: Australia halted military aid to Cambodia on Tuesday to increase pressure on strongman Hun Sen to restore constitutional rule and honour a pledge to hold free and fair elections.

But Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said cabinet had decided that the A$32 million a year (US$23.7 million) general aid programme to the impoverished southeast Asian country would continue for humanitarian reasons.

"The government has made clear its view that Hun Sen's overthrow of his coalition partner and first prime minister Prince (Norodom) Ranariddh by military action was completely unacceptable," Downer told reporters.

Australia provides about A$2 million a year in military assistance, mainly for English language training, communications training and to maintain Cambodia's small number of patrol boats. But military aid personnel will remain in Cambodia.
Downer did not say how soon military aid might be resumed.
But while Tuesday's announcement increased pressure on Hun Sen to restore constitutional rule, Downer dropped previous demands that Ranariddh be returned to power.
The United States, citing Hun Sen's "military victory", on Monday also declined to insist on Ranariddh's return. Washington last week suspended all aid to Cambodia for 30 days.
Australian ambassador to Cambodia Tony Kevin, in a leaked diplomatic cable, has urged Canberra to back Hun Sen, describing the former power-sharing arrangement as sterile and unworkable.

According to a weekend newspaper report citing the cable, Kevin said Hun Sen remained a democrat at heart and was seeking to restore stable government. He also said Hun Sen could be pressed to honour his commitment to free and fair elections if the right kind of pressure was applied.
Australia officially recognises states, not particular administrations, so formal recognition of the new administration is not an issue.

But Downer said Canberra's Cambodia policy and relations with Phnom Penh would be determined by Cambodia's attitude to 1991 peace accords, the holding of free elections, and the inclusion in government of Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party.

He said he had received assurances on these issues from his Cambodian counterpart, Ung Huot, through Phnom Penh's ambbasador to Australia, Vun Chheang. Ung Huot, a Royalist ally of the ousted Ranariddh, returned to Phnom Penh on Monday.
"The message I've had from Ung Huot today is heartening, but we'd like to see the results on the ground," Downer said.

Hun Sen and Ranariddh formed their power-sharing coalition after U.N.-organised elections in May 1993 which Ranariddh won. Never a happy alliance, the coalition began falling apart last year when Ranariddh demanded more power in the provinces.
